title: 22. Interview: Reliability
summary: Interview Q&A for Reliability — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Reliability interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between reliability and availability, and why does it matter for SLOs?
**Answer:** Availability is the fraction of time the system is up: `A = uptime / (uptime + downtime)`. Reliability is broader — it asks whether the system produced correct results under the conditions promised, for the entire duration. A payment gateway that is up 100% but silently drops 0.1% of transactions is available but not reliable. For SLOs this distinction matters because availability captures only outages, while reliability captures correctness bugs, data corruption, partial failures, and degraded behavior. SLOs typically split the two: an availability SLO ("99.95% uptime") and a reliability SLO ("99.99% of requests return correct results"). Conflating them leads to dashboards that look green while customers are losing money. A robust SLO framework tracks both, plus latency, and feeds them into a shared error budget that gates releases.
**Visual:**
```
Availability:  was it up?       |████████████████████| 99.95%
Reliability:   was it right?    |███████████████░██░░| 99.91%  <- hidden bug
```

### Q2. Explain MTBF and MTTR. How does each contribute to availability?
**Answer:** MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average uptime between two consecutive failures. MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery) is the average time to restore service after a failure. Availability is `A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)`. You can improve availability by either increasing MTBF (failing less often — better hardware, fewer bug deploys, redundancy) or decreasing MTTR (recovering faster — automated failover, blue-green deploys, runbooks, self-healing). Cloud-native culture deliberately targets MTTR because driving MTBF to infinity is impossible and expensive, while reducing MTTR from hours to seconds is achievable with engineering. Netflix's Chaos Monkey is explicitly an MTTR exercise: by forcing failures daily, teams prove their recovery paths work and stay tight. For example, going from MTBF=1000h/MTTR=4h (99.6%) to MTTR=4min (99.993%) is a 100x availability improvement without changing how often failures occur.
**Visual:**
```
MTBF: |=========uptime=========|X|=down=|
                                    ^--- MTTR
A = uptime / (uptime + down)
```

### Q3. Compare active-active and active-passive redundancy. When would you choose each?
**Answer:** Active-active runs multiple replicas serving live traffic simultaneously; if one fails, others continue with no visible gap. It gives the lowest MTTR (effectively zero, since surviving replicas already serve) and the highest throughput because all capacity is utilized. The cost is consistency: replicas must agree on state, which requires consensus (Raft, Paxos) or eventual consistency, and engineers must handle split-brain. Active-passive runs one primary serving traffic while one or more standbys wait; on failure the standby is promoted. It is simpler — no concurrent writes, no consensus needed for the primary path — but promotion adds seconds to minutes of MTTR and wastes standby capacity. Choose active-active for stateless read-heavy services (CDNs, API frontends, read replicas) and for systems with strong consistency tooling (Spanner, CockroachDB). Choose active-passive for stateful systems where simplicity and consistency matter more than failover speed (PostgreSQL streaming replication, Redis Sentinel, traditional RDBMS DR setups).
**Visual:**
```
Active-Active:        Active-Passive:
  [A live]<-->[B live]   [A live]  [B standby]
     both serve           only A serves
   failover: instant     failover: promote B (~10s-min)
```

### Q4. What is graceful degradation, and how does Netflix apply it to video playback?
**Answer:** Graceful degradation is the design pattern where a system, on losing a non-critical dependency, continues serving the critical path with reduced functionality rather than failing entirely. Netflix's playback page has many subsystems: personalized recommendations, artwork personalization, subtitles, chapter markers, ratings, preview trailers. None of these are required to actually start playing the video. When the recommendation service times out, Netflix falls back to a cached "trending now" list; when artwork personalization fails, it uses a default hero image; when the ratings service is down, it hides the star rating. The video itself keeps playing. This requires engineers to rank features by criticality at design time, build explicit fallbacks, and test that fallbacks actually work under realistic failure. The pitfall is silent shared dependencies — if every fallback ultimately calls the same identity service, the page still goes dark when identity fails. Dependency mapping is essential.
**Visual:**
```
[Recommendations]--X--> fallback: cached trending
[Artwork]         --X--> fallback: default image
[Ratings]         --X--> fallback: hide widget
[Video stream]    ----> MUST WORK  -->  play()
```

### Q5. What is an error budget, and how does it trade reliability against velocity?
**Answer:** An error budget is the inverse of an SLO: if your SLO is 99.9% availability, you have a 0.1% error budget per measurement window — about 43 minutes of downtime per month. As long as you stay under that budget, you are allowed to take risks (deploy new code, push features, run experiments). When the budget is exhausted, all further changes are frozen until the budget regenerates or the window resets. This converts reliability from a vague "as reliable as possible" goal into a quantified contract between the SRE team and product teams. Without error budgets, reliability becomes a political fight: SREs want 100%, product wants to ship. With them, both sides agree on a number and the budget self-governs releases. Google popularized this in SRE practice; Amazon and Netflix use variants of it. The trade-off: a tighter SLO means less room to experiment and slower feature velocity; a looser one means more incidents visible to users.
**Visual:**
```
SLO 99.9%  ->  budget = 43 min/month
Month budget: |=========budget used========|---- remaining ----|
                                                  releases OK
Month budget: |==============================|X overspent
                                                  freeze releases
```

### Q6. What is the role of chaos engineering in improving reliability?
**Answer:** Chaos engineering is the discipline of running controlled failure experiments in production to validate that the system actually degrades gracefully when components fail. Rather than relying on tests that prove the system works when everything is healthy, chaos experiments prove it survives when things break. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances during business hours; Latency Monkey injects network delays between services; Conformity Monkey flags instances that don't meet tagging or configuration standards. The goal is not to break the system — it is to surface hidden coupling, missing fallbacks, and stale runbooks before a real outage does. Chaos engineering raises MTBF indirectly (by surfacing bugs that would have caused failures) and lowers MTTR dramatically (by forcing teams to build and test recovery paths). The pitfall is running chaos without a kill switch or without observability — a chaos experiment that triggers a real outage without anyone noticing defeats the purpose.
**Visual:**
```
[Prod cluster]
   |--- Chaos Monkey: kill random pod
   |--- Latency Monkey: inject 500ms
   |--- Conformity Monkey: audit tags
       |
       v
   Observability dashboard catches fallback failures
       |
       v
   Fix hidden coupling BEFORE real outage
```

### Q7. Why is 100% reliability a bad target, and how do senior engineers choose the right reliability level?
**Answer:** 100% reliability is mathematically impossible at finite cost — every component has a non-zero failure rate, and at scale rare failures become frequent. Chasing the last nine also incurs an order-of-magnitude cost increase per nine, plus it eliminates the error budget, which freezes feature velocity. Senior engineers instead pick the reliability target that matches the business cost of failure. A bank's core ledger targets five nines because a single wrong transaction is a regulatory event. A recommendation service targets three nines because a missed recommendation costs pennies. The decision framework: estimate the cost of an outage (lost revenue, SLA penalty, churn), divide by the cost of the next nine, and stop where marginal cost exceeds marginal value. Document this explicitly so future engineers don't reflexively add another nine. The right reliability level is the one the business can defend, not the highest achievable number.
**Visual:**
```
Reliability  Cost       Marginal value
99%          $          acceptable for content feeds
99.9%        $$         OK for most user-facing APIs
99.99%       $$$$       required for payments
99.999%      $$$$$$$$$  only nuclear/medical/aerospace
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run Amazon's checkout service. During Prime Day, traffic spikes 4x and one of your three regions starts showing elevated error rates. What do you do?
**Answer:** The checkout service is Amazon's most reliability-critical path — it must not go down, and it must not silently drop or double-charge orders. The first move is to shift traffic away from the degraded region using the global load balancer (Route 53 weighted routing or an internal equivalent), draining it gracefully so in-flight transactions complete. Simultaneously, scale the other two regions up to absorb the load — checkout is mostly stateless except for the final transaction commit, which is delegated to a strongly consistent payment backend. Do not attempt to debug the degraded region during the peak; freeze changes, capture diagnostics, and isolate it. If the degraded region's failure rate exceeds threshold, mark it unhealthy and let active-active failover handle it. Post-incident, run a blameless post-mortem to find root cause and add it to the chaos engineering suite so the next Prime Day is resilient to it. The principle: protect the customer-facing critical path first, debug after.
**Visual:**
```
[Region A] errors  [Region B] healthy  [Region C] healthy
      \                |                   /
       \--- drain -----+---- scale up ----/
        v
   Global LB: 0% / 50% / 50%
```

### Q2. Your team runs a notification service that has 99.9% availability but users complain notifications are sometimes delayed by 20+ minutes. How do you diagnose and improve reliability?
**Answer:** Availability of 99.9% measures only whether the service was up; it does not capture whether notifications were delivered within the user-expected SLA. The complaint points to a reliability gap, not an availability gap. Start by adding latency and end-to-end delivery SLOs: "99% of notifications delivered within 30 seconds." Instrument the pipeline: producer → queue → worker → push gateway → device. The 20-minute delay is likely a queue backlog (workers not scaling fast enough) or a downstream push gateway throttling. Add per-stage latency metrics and p99 dashboards. Likely fixes: autoscale workers based on queue depth, add priority queues for time-sensitive notifications (2FA codes vs marketing), implement dead-letter queues for undeliverable notifications, and add a backpressure mechanism so producers slow down when queues grow. Also check for GC pauses in the worker JVM, which often cause periodic 10-30s stalls invisible in average metrics but visible in p99. Update the SLO to capture delivery latency, not just uptime.
**Visual:**
```
producer -> [queue 100k deep] -> [5 workers] -> push
              ^--- backlog here    ^--- scale to 50
```

### Q3. Netflix wants to add a new "Skip Intro" feature to playback. The recommendation team wants to personalize it based on viewing history. How do you design it for reliability without coupling playback to recommendations?
**Answer:** The Skip Intro button is on the critical playback path; the recommendation service is not. Coupling them would mean a recommendation outage breaks playback — unacceptable. Design it as a two-tier feature: the core Skip Intro button uses static intro timestamps stored on the video metadata service (which is already on the critical path and highly reliable). Personalization (which intros to suggest skipping next, which shows to recommend after skip) is a non-critical enhancement served by the recommendation service with a 200ms timeout and a fallback. If the recommendation service responds, enrich the Skip Intro payload; if not, return the static version. Cache recommendation results on the client for 5 minutes to absorb short outages. Track both paths separately in dashboards so you can see when personalization is degraded without alarming on the playback SLO. This pattern — critical path with optional enrichment — is how Netflix structures every playback feature, and it is what lets them degrade gracefully during partial failures.
**Visual:**
```
[Play] -> [metadata Svc: intro ts] --> [skip button: WORKS]
                  |
                  +--> [rec Svc: 200ms timeout]
                          |           |
                       ok |           v timeout
                          v           fallback: static
                       enrich
```

### Q4. Your startup's payment service has MTBF of 200 hours and MTTR of 30 minutes. The business wants 99.99% availability. How do you close the gap?
**Answer:** Current availability is `200 / (200 + 0.5) = 99.75%`, which is two nines. The target of 99.99% (four nines) requires ~52 minutes of downtime per year, but at MTBF=200h you fail ~44 times per year, and even at MTTR=30min that's 22 hours of downtime — 25x over budget. You cannot close this gap by reducing MTTR alone; you must raise MTBF dramatically. Steps: (1) Eliminate the root causes of the 200h failures — these are bugs, config errors, or capacity issues. Add canary deploys, automated rollback, and pre-prod integration tests to catch bugs before prod. (2) Add redundancy: move from single-instance to active-active across two AZs, so a single instance failure no longer counts as a service failure. (3) Reduce MTTR from 30 min to under 1 min via automated health checks, blue-green deploys, and runbook automation. With active-active, individual instance failures (MTBF=200h per instance) become invisible to the service, and service-level MTBF jumps to thousands of hours. Combined with sub-minute MTTR, you reach four nines. Be honest with the business: 99.99% requires sustained engineering investment, not a one-time fix.
**Visual:**
```
Now:   MTBF 200h, MTTR 30min  ->  99.75% (2 nines)
Goal:  MTBF 10000h, MTTR 1min ->  99.9998% (5 nines) -- overshoots
       MTBF 5000h,  MTTR 5min ->  99.998%  (4 nines) -- on target
```

### Q5. You are deploying a new microservice. The DBA team insists on active-passive Postgres replication for safety; the SRE team wants active-active via CockroachDB. How do you decide?
**Answer:** Frame the decision around the workload's tolerance for failover gaps, consistency needs, and team expertise. Active-passive Postgres is operationally mature, supports strong consistency trivially (one writer), and has a well-understood failover path via Patroni or Stolon — but it incurs 10–60 seconds of downtime during promotion, which violates SLOs for latency-sensitive services. Active-active via CockroachDB gives multi-writer multi-region capability with near-zero failover gap, but at the cost of higher write latency (Raft consensus per write) and operational novelty for the team. Ask: does the business need <5s failover? Is the team staffed to operate a distributed SQL database? Are writes latency-sensitive (favor single-region active-passive) or geo-distributed (favor multi-region active-active)? If the service is single-region and the team is small, choose Postgres active-passive and accept the 30s failover in the SLO. If the service is multi-region customer-facing (e.g., global checkout), CockroachDB's complexity is justified. There is no universally correct answer — the decision is a trade-off between failover speed, write latency, and operational cost.
**Visual:**
```
Active-Passive Postgres        Active-Active CockroachDB
  failover: 10-60s               failover: ~0s
  write latency: low             write latency: higher (Raft)
  ops maturity: high             ops maturity: medium
  region: single                 region: multi
```

### Q6. A junior engineer proposes adding circuit breakers to every downstream call to "improve reliability." What feedback do you give?
**Answer:** Circuit breakers are a powerful pattern but applying them blindly to every call is an anti-pattern. Circuit breakers are appropriate when a downstream service is slow or failing and continuing to call it worsens the situation — e.g., exhausting connection pools, amplifying retries, or causing cascading failures. They are inappropriate for cheap, fast, idempotent calls where the cost of opening the circuit (returning an error to the caller) exceeds the cost of just letting the call fail. The feedback: (1) For each downstream call, identify the failure mode — does a slow downstream cause resource exhaustion upstream? If yes, circuit breaker. If no, a simple timeout suffices. (2) Tune thresholds carefully — too sensitive and the breaker trips on normal latency variance; too lax and it never trips. (3) Pair every circuit breaker with a fallback (cached value, default, or graceful degradation) so opening the circuit doesn't simply propagate the failure. (4) Add metrics and alerts so you know when breakers are open — a half-open breaker is a sign of an upstream problem worth investigating, not a "normal" state. (5) Test under realistic load — many circuit breakers never fire in pre-prod and turn out to be misconfigured when they finally do.
**Visual:**
```
[caller] --[breaker]--> [slow downstream]
   |                        |
   |  trips on N failures   |
   v                        v
fallback         downstream recovers
                       v
                 half-open: probe
```

### Q7. Your team's SLO dashboard shows 99.95% availability but the error budget is exhausted three weeks into the month. The product team wants to ship a major feature. What do you do?
**Answer:** The error budget contract exists precisely for this situation: when the budget is exhausted, releases freeze until the budget regenerates (next window) or the SLO is renegotiated. The right answer is to hold the release, investigate why the budget was burned (root-cause the incidents), and ship only after either the budget recovers or the business formally accepts the risk and raises the SLO breach to a documented exception. Concretely: (1) Freeze non-emergency production changes — feature flags can still be merged but not enabled. (2) Run a blameless post-mortem on each budget-burning incident; if they share a root cause, prioritize the fix. (3) If the feature is genuinely time-critical (e.g., a regulatory deadline), escalate to leadership and document a one-time exception with explicit risk acknowledgment. (4) Re-evaluate whether the SLO is set correctly — if the team consistently burns the budget, the SLO may be too tight or the underlying system may need architectural investment. The discipline of freezing on budget exhaustion is what makes error budgets meaningful; without it, they are just decoration.
**Visual:**
```
Budget: |========burned========|---- exhausted ----|
                                     ^
                                     freeze releases
                                     root-cause incidents
                                     renegotiate SLO if chronic
```
